title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: pronouns, prepositions and a text to read

questions.prompt: Rewrite this sentence with pronouns in the place of the names: "Nabil showed Nabil's photographs to Amira and Sonia." Which version is correct?

options.text: He showed him photographs to them.
He showed his photographs to them.
He showed his photographs to they.
Him showed his photographs to them.

questions.explanation: Nabil does the action, so the subject form opens the sentence; the photographs belong to him, so a possessive comes immediately before the noun; and "to" is a preposition, which forces the object form: He showed his photographs to them. The classic mistake is "He showed his photographs to they.", where a subject form is left standing after a preposition. "Him showed his photographs to them." puts an object form before the verb, and "He showed him photographs to them." uses an object form where a possessive is needed in front of "photographs".

questions.prompt: Complete: "The chef waited ___ the door of the hotel, put the box ___ the table and finished the sauce ___ the kitchen."

options.text: at ... on ... in
in ... on ... at
on ... at ... in
on ... in ... at

questions.explanation: A door is an exact point in space, a table is a surface, and a kitchen is something you stand inside, which gives at ... on ... in. "in ... on ... at" sends the chef inside the door itself and then treats the kitchen as a point on a map. "on ... at ... in" leaves the chef standing on the door, and "on ... in ... at" adds a box buried inside the table.

questions.prompt: Read this passage. "Rania Cherif has run a small pharmacy in Béja since 2021. Her aunt Nejia sold medicines in the same street for twenty years, and Salwa, the assistant that Rania trained, opens the shop at seven every morning. Last winter the flu filled the waiting room for a month. Nejia came back behind the counter for three weeks and refused to take a single dinar. Salwa never left before nine, and at the end of the month Rania paid her a full extra week's wages and thanked them both in front of the customers." In the last sentence, who does "her" point at, and who does "them" point at?

options.text: her = Nejia, them = Nejia and Salwa
her = Nejia, them = Salwa and Rania
her = Salwa, them = Nejia and Salwa
her = Salwa, them = Salwa and Rania

questions.explanation: Nejia refused to take a single dinar, so she cannot be the one who is paid; the extra week rewards Salwa, who never left before nine, and "both" covers the two women who helped: her = Salwa, them = Nejia and Salwa. The classic mistake is to jump back to Nejia, the helper of the sentence before, without asking who can be paid at all; the rule of the lesson points the other way, since the nearest woman named before "her" is Salwa, who opens the shop and never leaves before nine. Rania is the subject who pays and thanks, so "them" can never include her, and the customers only watch the scene.

questions.prompt: Read what Wassim says, then fill in the line "Family size" of his file, which counts the people living under the same roof. "I'm Wassim, I'm eighteen, and I still live at home while I study at a cookery school in Nabeul. There are also my father, my mother, my grandmother, my two sisters and my little brother. My elder brother left for Sfax two years ago and only comes back in August. My father works in a shoe factory, and my mother teaches at the primary school." How many people live in his home?

options.text: Five people.
Six people.
Seven people.
Eight people.

questions.explanation: Wassim never gives a total: he lists his father, his mother, his grandmother, his two sisters and his little brother, which makes six, and he lives there too, so the file reads Seven people. Adding the elder brother gives eight, but that brother left for Sfax two years ago and only visits in August. Forgetting to count Wassim himself gives six, and forgetting Wassim as well as reading "my two sisters" as one person gives five.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Rachid drove ___ mother to the wedding, and she thanked ___ twice."

options.text: his ... him
his ... he
her ... him
her ... he

questions.explanation: A possessive adjective follows the owner, and the owner here is Rachid, so the mother is "his mother"; after the verb "thanked" English needs an object form, which gives his ... him. The classic mistake is "her ... him", which makes the possessive agree with the woman it stands in front of instead of with Rachid, the owner. "his ... he" puts a subject form straight after the verb, and "her ... he" gets both columns wrong at once.

questions.prompt: Nadia took charge of her own kitchen at twenty-two. She writes: "The first year was a struggle, but I never asked my parents for a dinar." Which sentence says exactly the same thing?

options.text: Her first year was easy, and her parents paid for it.
Her parents helped her through a very hard first year.
She gave up when the first year became too hard.
The first year was hard, and she paid for it herself.

questions.explanation: A struggle is a hard fight or effort, and asking nobody for a dinar means that the money came from her alone, which gives "The first year was hard, and she paid for it herself." "Her parents helped her through a very hard first year." keeps the hard year but hands her the help she says she refused, and "Her first year was easy, and her parents paid for it." misses both halves of the sentence. "She gave up when the first year became too hard." invents an ending, since a struggle is something you go through, not something you lose.
